Being First Lady is actually an executive position, but the ineligibility clause prevents a person in the executive branch from serving in Congress:

The ineligibility clause could also be considered relevant to Hillary Clinton's run for Senate in 2000. Although the First Lady of the United States receives no salary, she holds spending and hiring authority concerning areas under her White House East Wing and residence purview. Her daughter, Chelsea Clinton, often served as White House hostess or de facto acting First Lady during Clinton's Senatorial campaign as Hillary Clinton needed to set aside her First Lady duties as she ran for senate. She had to set aside her duties as First Lady in part because she needed to move to the state of New York to establish residency there. She resumed her duties as First Lady when she won her senate campaign. For the fortnight between Hillary Clinton taking office as a Senator (January 3, 2001) and the expiration of Bill Clinton's presidency (January 20, 2001), Hillary Clinton remained first lady.

Otherwise, of course she can be president. The only two limitations to being president regarding previous positions is that the person must not have been elected president twice, or, in the case of a person who has served in place of another president for more than two years, must not have been elected once.

Category Hasn't served for anyone else Has served for someone else, but for less than 2 years Has served for someone else, but for more than 2 years
Restrictions Can only be elected to two terms Can only be elected to two terms Can be elected only once
Maximum time 8 years 8-10 years 6 years
Examples - Lyndon B. Johnson, but didn't rerun for "3rd" term Ford, but didn't run for "2nd" term

One quirk is that a person can serve as President indefinitely if he's elected VP and each President steps down, resigns or is deemed unfit.
